I value safe, effective access to women’s health care—care grounded in evidence, ethics, and respect for patients. That’s why I oppose efforts to eliminate abortion care for veterans, even in cases of rape, incest, or threats to the life or health of the pregnant person; ban VA clinicians from even discussing abortion options with their patients; and strip coverage from CHAMPVA recipients, including spouses and dependents of disabled veterans.

This isn’t about law—it’s about ideology overriding medicine. The Biden-era VA policy (September 2022) allowed abortion counseling and, in limited cases, abortion care when a veteran’s life or health is endangered or the pregnancy resulted from rape or incest—an approach aligned with evidence-based practice and the urgent health needs of veterans.

Today, the proposed reversal would reinstate a near-total exclusion on abortions and abortion counseling in VA care and in CHAMPVA, rolling back those patient protections and even restricting what VA doctors can say to their patients. That’s a dangerous departure from patient-centered medicine.

When access is eliminated, people suffer preventable harm. The World Health Organization is unequivocal: lack of access to safe, timely abortion care drives unsafe procedures that contribute substantially to maternal injuries and deaths worldwide.  In the U.S., emerging post-Dobbs research links restrictive abortion laws to worse outcomes. For example, a 2025 JAMA analysis found higher-than-expected infant mortality in states after adoption of abortion bans, with increases tied especially to congenital anomalies—signals of delayed or denied care.  Rigorous studies and clinician reports also document delays in miscarriage and medically indicated pregnancy care under bans—patients are kept sicker, longer, while clinicians navigate legal threats instead of practicing best-evidence medicine.

Veterans and their families deserve better, not gag rules and coverage carve-outs. The VA’s 2022 policy was built on evidence and precedent to ensure that, in dire circumstances—rape, incest, or threats to the life or health of the pregnant veteran—care and counseling would be available. Reinstating blanket exclusions at VA and CHAMPVA would erase those protections and predictably increase the risk of permanent harm or death for patients who need time-sensitive care.

Most Americans agree that reproductive decisions should remain with patients and their clinicians. National polling by Pew Research Center in 2024 found that about six in ten U.S. adults say abortion should be legal in all or most cases—support that has grown since 2021.

I stand with veterans, families, and frontline clinicians. Health care policy should reduce risk, not create it; it should empower informed conversations, not silence them. Rolling back evidence-based VA and CHAMPVA protections puts ideology ahead of patient safety. We should keep—and strengthen—policies that protect veterans’ health and uphold their dignity.
